title: GitHub - paveluv/e: A fully customizable self-aware Emacs-like editor written in Chez Scheme.
excerpt: A fully customizable self-aware Emacs-like editor written in Chez Scheme. - paveluv/e
content_html:
e is a tiny Emacs-like console editor written in Chez Scheme. It feels like Emacs in many ways (buffers, recursive window splits, incremental search, built-in Scheme), but it's not trying to be an Emacs clone.

The editor is itself a Scheme system. It's a set of R6RS libraries, all of which, except the core, are hot-reloadable. Editing and saving a module from within e applies the changes immediately.

Highlights:

  • M-x evaluates Scheme in the editor's context, with structural multiline input, semantic completion, parameter hints, history, and captured output (evaluation results, stdout, and stderr are captured separately).
  • Besides normal editing buffers, there are app buffers. They update their presentation from internal structures and can optionally interact with the user (*log*, *git-log*, *buffers*, *terminal*).
  • Windows form a recursive tiling layout that is easy to reshape: split in either direction (C-x 2, C-x 3), drag edges with a mouse, or widen any edge from the keyboard (C-x w).
  • C-c t turns the current buffer into a PTY-backed terminal able to run shells, full-screen programs, or another editor such as legmacs.
  • Undo and redo describe meaningful edits: typed runs, pastes, replacements, and formatter passes.
  • There are no dependencies beyond Chez Scheme, a Unix-like terminal, and the system libc.so. The first start automatically compiles its libraries; later starts are typically around 100 ms.

Start

e is intended to be installed from source in your home directory. There are no prebuilt binaries or packages. Stable Git tags will be created once it matures.

Install as a personal editor:

$ git clone https://github.com/paveluv/e ~/.e
$ ~/.e/e file.txt

Or vendor it inside a project so the editor and project-specific extensions travel with the source:

$ git clone https://github.com/paveluv/e ~/git/project/.e
$ rm -rf ~/git/project/.e/.git
$ ~/git/project/.e/e file.txt

Each installation is self-contained. It uses the lib/, config.e, data/, and compiled eo/ beside its own loader.

On FreeBSD, where Chez installs a differently named script interpreter, run chez-scheme --script e or change the shebang as explained in the loader.

Essential keys

Key Action
C-x C-f Find a file
C-x C-s Save
C-x C-w Save as
C-x C-c Quit safely
C-x b Switch buffers by name
C-x C-b Switch through the interactive *buffers* table
C-x 2, C-x 3 Split the current window below or right
C-x 0, C-x 1 Delete this window or every other window
M-Arrows Move between windows along the cursor's screen ray
C-x w Widen window edges; use Meta+Arrow to choose another window
C-s Incremental search
M-% Query replace
C-_, C-M-_ Undo, redo
C-@, C-w, M-w, C-y Mark, kill, copy, yank
M-x Evaluate Scheme interactively
C-x C-e Evaluate the current buffer as Scheme
C-h f, M-., C-h k Describe a name, symbol at point, or key
C-x g Browse Git history and patches
C-c t Open a terminal buffer
C-g, Escape Cancel the current interaction

Scheme at the center

The live top-level environment exposes the published editor API and loaded modules. You can call it via M-x:

M-x (buffer-name (current-buffer))
M-x (replace-all! "old" "new" buffer-file)
M-x (log-view 'eval)
M-x (terminal!!)
M-x (describe terminal!!)

(The double-bang suffix !! means that the command is interactive.)

Configuration is Scheme too. Copy config.template.e to config.e, uncomment the settings worth changing, and save it; the running editor applies it immediately.

Documentation

  • Buffers and windows: files, splits, scrolling, line numbers, scrollbars, mouse behavior, *buffers*, and the buffer API.
  • Evaluation: M-x, eval!, multiline commands, output capture, interruption, history, and result copying.
  • Terminal buffers: capture, escape, emulation, scrollback, titles, process lifetime, and the terminal API.
  • Search and replacement: incremental search, smart case, query replace, and structured replacement targets.
  • Indentation and formatting: Scheme layout, conservative and intrusive formatting, save hooks, and the CLI formatter.
  • Interactive prompts: editing, multiline input, completion, styling, suggestions, and prompt APIs.
  • Echo area and log: structured messages, progress, histories, formatters, and dynamic log views.
  • Describe: live reference pages, key discovery, corpus installation, structured queries, and module-published documentation.
  • Configuration: reload semantics, precedence, and common settings.
  • Key bindings: key syntax, contextual maps, overrides, unbinding, and inspection.
  • Styles: the style DSL, faces, colors, terminal behavior, and configuration lifecycle.
  • App buffers: dynamic views, interaction, capture, mouse events, and target windows.
  • Git: structured repository queries and the history browser.
  • Pretty Scheme: structural delimiter glyphs, depth and rainbow variants, and semantic symbol styling.
  • Modules and architecture: library boundaries, hot reload, registrations, modes, highlighters, and extension conventions.

Limits

Tabs and other control characters display as one space cell. Input is UTF-8, but e currently assumes every character occupies one terminal column.

Licence

MIT
